newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Beleagured Yeltsin, Lebed to meet on Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Beleagured Yeltsin, Lebed to meet on Chechnya.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday discusses the faltering Chechnya peace process face-to-face with his ambitious security chief Alexander Lebed for the first time amid a barrage of attacks on both men.
Yeltsin, in hospital preparing for heart surgery, came under fire from opposition leaders in parliament on Wednesday for refusing to give up power despite his health problems.

His press service said he would meet Lebed -- who signed a controversial peace deal with Chechnya's rebels -- in the Central Clinical Hospital where he has been for the past two weeks, preparing for his operation.
Aside from Chechnya, Yeltsin faces a new wave of criticism on Thursday -- the third anniversary of a rebellion by the old parliament which he put down with tanks.

Lebed walked out of the beginning of a new parliamentary session on Wednesday after deputies heckled and jeered him for the agreement he signed with Chechnya's rebels in August to end 21 months of fighting which killed tens of thousands.
A ceasefire has held but the withdrawal of Russian troops from the region envisaged by the deal is proceeding slowly amid concern in Moscow that the rebels have got away with too much.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, adding his voice to a chorus of condemnation for the agreement, won thunderous applause for a speech in which he said Lebed's agreement was a humiliating step towards Russia's disintegration.
Rebel leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev is due to fly to Moscow on Thursday to meet Lebed and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and sign a document, said a Swiss mediator in Chechnya.

Tim Guldimann from the Organisation For Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) did not give details and it was not clear what sort of compromise could be reached in the atmosphere of heated defiance on both sides.

Yandarbiyev has repeated rebel insistence on independence for the North Caucasus region and Chernomyrdin, whose office had earlier dismissed talk of a meeting with the rebel leader, has responded cooly to the peace deal.

Chernomyrdin, who has taken over some of Yeltsin's powers in the run-up to the heart operation due in the next six to ten weeks, has previously played go-between with Lebed over Chechnya, which he insists must stay in the Russian Federation.
But Yeltsin has boosted his political profile in the past few days as his aides fight charges that Russia is rudderless.

Presidential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais said on Wednesday that the 65-year-old Kremlin leader was in full control and that he had reorganised Yeltsin's administration to make sure presidential orders were carried out.

Chubais took a swipe at Lebed -- seen as one of his main rivals since Yeltsin's illness -- and made clear that the president was reining in his security chief, saying he had appointed a man opposed by Lebed to supervise army appointments.
He said anyone thinking Yeltsin's illness meant it was time to manoeuvre for power would find they were acting prematurely.

But the leader of the powerful Communist Party Gennady Zyuganov said that no-one was ruling the country, which was in dire need of measures to resolve a social crisis over unpaid wages in the huge and cash-strapped state sector.
"The government is unable to resolve a single question," said Zyuganov. "If things go on like this Russia will repeat the fate of the Soviet Union."

Zyuganov's backers plan to hold rallies around Moscow's television tower on Thursday to mark the 1993 Moscow confrontation between security forces and supporters of the hardline parliamentarians Yeltsin accused of blocking reforms.
More than 120 people were killed in the clash and subsequent battles around the White House parliament building before Yeltsin defeated his political foes.
His present-day parliamentary opponents are again on the offensive -- they plan to try set up a medical commission on Friday to review his ability to rule.
But in the Kremlin-dominated political system Yeltsin managed to push through after the October 1993 events, it is not clear how far they will get.
